note:
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 42-year-old female admitted with community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe. She presented 3 days before admission with productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. This morning she says the cough is less productive and the chest pain is much better. She denies hemoptysis, denies nausea or vomiting, and reports no diarrhea. She has not had any new shortness of breath at rest. Her past history includes mild persistent asthma, which has been quiet; she used her albuterol inhaler twice yesterday but not since last night. She has no known drug allergies.

Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours, azithromycin 500 mg IV every 24 hours, albuterol 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE prophylaxis.

Vitals this morning: temperature 37.6 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. She required 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula on admission and was weaned to room air yesterday afternoon. On exam she is comfortable and speaking in full sentences. There are crackles at the right base with no wheeze. Heart rhythm is regular, and she has no peripheral edema.

Data review: white blood cell count was 14.2 on admission and is 10.1 today, and creatinine is 0.8. The admission chest x-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. Blood cultures have shown no growth at 48 hours, the sputum culture grew only normal oral flora, and the urine Legionella antigen was negative.

Impression: community-acquired pneumonia, clinically improving, off oxygen and without fever for 24 hours. Her mild persistent asthma is stable.

Plan for today is to stop the IV ceftriaxone and switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily to complete a total of 5 days of antibiotics. The third and final dose of IV azithromycin will be given today and then it will be stopped. Continue albuterol as needed and stop enoxaparin at discharge. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if she remains stable on room air. She will repeat a chest x-ray in 6 weeks, and I discussed return precautions with her.
summary: A 42-year-old female with mild persistent asthma is on hospital day 3 for community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe. She is improving, with less cough and chest pain, no fever for 24 hours and weaning to room air, and her white blood cell count has fallen from 14.2 to 10.1. The admission chest x-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation, and blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours. The impression is improving pneumonia with stable asthma. IV ceftriaxone is being switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, IV azithromycin ends after today's dose, and discharge is anticipated tomorrow with a repeat chest x-ray in 6 weeks.

Cough is less productive and chest pain much better this morning. Denies hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and new shortness of breath at rest. History of mild persistent asthma; used albuterol twice yesterday but not since last night. No known drug allergies.

Comfortable, speaking in full sentences, crackles at the right base, no wheeze, regular rhythm, no peripheral edema. White blood cell count 14.2 on admission and 10.1 today, creatinine 0.8. Admission chest x-ray with right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. Blood cultures no growth at 48 hours, sputum culture normal oral flora, urine Legionella antigen negative.

Give the third and final dose of IV azithromycin today, then stop

Return precautions discussed

Doctor: Good morning. I see your primary care doctor sent you because your PSA came back high. Let me confirm, you are a 72-year-old male and you work rotating shifts, is that right?
Patient: That's right. Some weeks I work nights and some weeks days, so my schedule is all over the place.
Doctor: Understood, we will plan around that. The PSA was elevated at 7.4. Are you having any trouble passing urine?
Patient: I get up twice a night to urinate, and the stream is weaker than it used to be. But no burning when I pee.
Doctor: Any blood in your urine?
Patient: No, I haven't seen any blood in my urine.
Doctor: Any bone pain or weight loss that you can't explain?
Patient: No bone pain, and no weight loss. My weight has been steady.
Doctor: Do you have any other health problems or take any medicines?
Patient: Just high blood pressure. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning after my shift.
Doctor: Okay. On the digital rectal exam today, your prostate is mildly enlarged, smooth, and symmetric, with no nodules.
Patient: Is that good?
Doctor: It is reassuring. My impression is an elevated PSA, most likely from an enlarged prostate, but we need to make sure it is not cancer. I want a repeat PSA and a urinalysis today, and if the PSA is still high, an MRI of the prostate.
Patient: Can the lab be done on my schedule?
Doctor: Yes, the lab is open until evening, and my staff will schedule the MRI at a time that fits your shifts. Please avoid vigorous exercise and sexual activity for two days before the blood draw. We will follow up in 3 weeks to go over the results.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 72-year-old male who works rotating shifts was referred for an elevated PSA of 7.4. He reports getting up twice a night to urinate and a weaker stream but denies burning, blood in the urine, bone pain and weight loss. He takes amlodipine 5 mg every morning for high blood pressure. The digital rectal exam showed a mildly enlarged, smooth, symmetric prostate without nodules, and the impression is an elevated PSA, most likely from an enlarged prostate. A repeat PSA and urinalysis will be done today, with an MRI of the prostate if the PSA stays high, scheduled around his shifts, and follow-up in 3 weeks.

soap.subjective: 72-year-old male with a rotating, irregular shift schedule referred for an elevated PSA of 7.4. Gets up twice a night to urinate and the stream is weaker than it used to be. soap.assessment: Elevated PSA, most likely from an enlarged prostate; cancer still needs to be excluded. High blood pressure.
plan: Repeat PSA and urinalysis today
MRI of the prostate if the PSA is still high
Schedule the MRI at a time that fits his shifts; lab open until evening
Avoid vigorous exercise and sexual activity for two days before the blood draw
Follow up in 3 weeks to review results

note:
Rheumatology clinic follow-up dictation for a 34-year-old female with fibromyalgia, last seen about 3 months ago. Her mother is here today as her family caregiver and is providing part of the history, because the patient has trouble recalling details when her fatigue and brain fog are bad. Chief complaint is ongoing widespread pain with poor sleep.

Interval history, the patient describes aching pain in the neck, shoulders, back and hips that she rates 7 out of 10 on bad days, with fatigue most of the day, brain fog and unrefreshing sleep. Her mother adds that she misses about one day of work each week and needs help with childcare on her bad days. Her mother also reports loud snoring at night. The patient has migraine headaches about twice a month and alternating constipation and loose stools. She denies joint swelling, rash, fever, dry eyes, dry mouth and mouth ulcers. She denies morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes and denies suicidal thoughts.

Past medical history includes fibromyalgia, depression, migraine, hypothyroidism and irritable bowel syndrome. She currently smokes about half a pack of cigarettes per day and has done so for 12 years.

Medications, and I want to be clear about this one. On arrival the patient said she was still taking pregabalin 75 mg twice a day. Her mother corrected her and said it was stopped about 3 weeks ago because of dizziness and weight gain. I confirmed this on the pharmacy refill history, so pregabalin is discontinued. Duloxetine was started at the last visit at 20 mg, correction, 30 mg daily, and she is tolerating it. She also takes levothyroxine 75 mcg daily and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for pain.

Vitals today, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 78, temperature 36.8 C, weight 164 pounds. On exam she is tired appearing but in no distress. She has diffuse tenderness at multiple soft tissue sites including the trapezius, lateral epicondyles and greater trochanters bilaterally. Widespread pain index is 13 and symptom severity score is 9. There is no synovitis in the hands, wrists, elbows, knees or ankles, no joint effusions, and no rash. Strength and reflexes are normal and range of motion is full.

Labs from 2 weeks ago reviewed, TSH 2.1, ESR 12, CRP normal, CBC normal with white blood cell count 6.8 and hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 0.7, and ANA negative.

Impression is fibromyalgia with inadequate control, with no evidence of inflammatory arthritis or connective tissue disease. Her hypothyroidism is well controlled. Her depression is stable. Ongoing tobacco use is a barrier to improvement.

Plan. First, increase duloxetine from 30 mg daily to 60 mg daily. Second, pregabalin stays discontinued and should not be restarted. Third, start cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime for sleep and muscle pain. Fourth, I counseled her on quitting smoking for several minutes, and she will start a nicotine patch 14 mg daily and I am referring her to the state quitline. Fifth, referral for cognitive behavioral therapy and a graded walking program starting at 10 minutes a day. Sixth, order a sleep study because of the snoring and unrefreshing sleep. Continue levothyroxine 75 mcg daily and acetaminophen as needed. Follow up in 8 weeks, sooner if her mood worsens. Her mother verbalized understanding of the plan.
summary: A 34-year-old female with fibromyalgia, depression, migraine, hypothyroidism and irritable bowel syndrome returned for follow-up with her mother, who helped provide the history. She has ongoing widespread pain, fatigue, brain fog and poor sleep, and she denies joint swelling, rash and fever. Pregabalin was already stopped about 3 weeks ago for dizziness and weight gain. Examination showed diffuse tenderness without synovitis, and recent TSH, ESR, CRP, CBC and ANA were normal or negative. The impression is fibromyalgia with inadequate control and ongoing tobacco use. Duloxetine is increased to 60 mg daily, cyclobenzaprine and a nicotine patch are started, and a sleep study and 8-week follow-up are planned.

Diffuse tenderness at multiple soft tissue sites including trapezius, lateral epicondyles and greater trochanters. Widespread pain index 13, symptom severity score 9. No synovitis, no joint effusions, no rash, normal strength and reflexes, full range of motion. Labs: TSH 2.1, ESR 12, CRP normal, CBC normal with white blood cell count 6.8 and hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 0.7, ANA negative.

plan: Increase duloxetine from 30 mg daily to 60 mg daily
Pregabalin remains discontinued and should not be restarted
Start cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime for sleep and muscle pain

note:
PULM CONSULT in ED, requested by ED attending for hypoxia in pt w/ known ILD.

46-year-old female, known RA-associated ILD (fibrotic NSIP pattern) dx 2 y ago, rheumatoid arthritis, HTN, GERD.
CC: progressive SOB x 2 wk, worse x 3 d.

HPI:
- DOE now ~1 block (baseline 3 blocks), new dry cough x 1 wk
- returned 6 d ago from 10-day international trip (Southeast Asia), 14 h flights each way, mostly seated
- works rotating night/day shifts at a distribution center, sleeps 4-5 h/d, admits missing meds on night shifts
- denies fever, chills, hemoptysis, CP, calf pain, orthopnea, diarrhea
- no known TB exposure, no sick contacts, no birds/mold at home
- never smoker, NKDA

Med rec (PTA):
- MTX: pt first stated 10 mg daily; clarified w/ pharmacy fill hx and rheum letter, MTX is 10 mg once WEEKLY (never daily)
- folic acid 1 mg daily
- hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BID
- prednisone 5 mg daily
- omeprazole 20 mg daily
- lisinopril 10 mg daily

ED vitals: T 37.1 C, HR 104, BP 138/84, RR 24, SpO2 88% on room air -> 94% on 3 L NC
Exam: tachypneic, speaking short sentences, bibasilar Velcro crackles, mild clubbing.
Neg: no wheeze, no JVD, no LE edema, calves nontender and symmetric.

Labs: WBC 9.8, Hgb 12.6, Plt 288, Na 138, K 4.1, Cr 0.8, BNP 62, troponin <0.01, lactate 1.3, procalcitonin 0.06, D-dimer 1.4 (elevated), flu/COVID/RSV PCR neg.
CXR: bibasilar reticular opacities, no consolidation, no effusion.
CTPA: no PE. Bibasilar subpleural reticulation w/ traction bronchiectasis (c/w known fibrosis) + new patchy bilateral GGO.

ED course: O2 3 L NC, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV x1, ceftriaxone 1 g IV x1 + azithromycin 500 mg IV x1 for possible superimposed CAP.

Imp:
1. Acute exacerbation of RA-ILD (new GGO on fibrotic background) w/ hypoxic resp failure
2. PE r/o by CTPA despite long flights
3. Infection unlikely: procal 0.06, viral PCR neg, no fever, WBC nl

Plan:
- admit to step-down for O2 titration, goal SpO2 >= 92%
- no further abx, ED doses only (infection unlikely)
- prednisone 40 mg PO daily starting tomorrow AM (was 5 mg daily)
- STOP MTX, rheum to decide on alternative DMARD
- continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BID, omeprazole 20 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily
- start TMP-SMX DS 1 tab MWF for PJP ppx while on pred >= 20 mg
- TTE to eval RV fxn; BMP + CBC in AM
- inpatient rheum consult; PFTs w/ DLCO once stable
- pillbox + phone alarms for meds around shift changes; pharmacy to give written med list
- flu + pneumococcal vaccines before d/c if not up to date
summary: A 46-year-old female with known RA-associated ILD, who works rotating shifts, presented to the ED with progressive shortness of breath and dry cough after returning from international travel. She was hypoxic at 88% on room air with bibasilar Velcro crackles and denied fever, chills, hemoptysis and calf pain. CTPA showed no PE but new bilateral ground-glass opacities on fibrotic lung, with a low procalcitonin and negative viral PCR. The impression is an acute exacerbation of RA-ILD with hypoxic respiratory failure, infection unlikely. She is admitted, MTX is stopped, prednisone is raised from 5 to 40 mg daily, TMP-SMX prophylaxis is started, and a TTE and rheumatology consult are planned.

soap.subjective: 46-year-old female with RA-associated ILD, rheumatoid arthritis, HTN and GERD with progressive shortness of breath for 2 weeks, worse for 3 days, dyspnea on exertion at about 1 block (baseline 3 blocks) and new dry cough for 1 week. Returned 6 days ago from a 10-day international trip with 14-hour flights each way. Works rotating night/day shifts at a distribution center, sleeps 4-5 hours a day and admits missing medications on night shifts. Denies fever, chills, hemoptysis, chest pain, calf pain, orthopnea and diarrhea; no known TB exposure or sick contacts; never smoker; no known drug allergies. Home medications: MTX 10 mg once weekly (patient first said daily, corrected by pharmacy fill history and rheumatology letter), folic acid 1 mg daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BID, prednisone 5 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily.
soap.objective: T 37.1 C, HR 104, BP 138/84, RR 24, SpO2 88% on room air improving to 94% on 3 L nasal cannula. Tachypneic, speaking short sentences, bibasilar Velcro crackles, mild clubbing; no wheeze, no JVD, no leg edema, calves nontender and symmetric. WBC 9.8, Hgb 12.6, Plt 288, Na 138, K 4.1, Cr 0.8, BNP 62, troponin <0.01, lactate 1.3, procalcitonin 0.06, D-dimer 1.4, flu/COVID/RSV PCR negative. CXR: bibasilar reticular opacities, no consolidation or effusion. CTPA: no PE, bibasilar subpleural reticulation with traction bronchiectasis consistent with known fibrosis and new patchy bilateral GGO. ED course: oxygen 3 L, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, ceftriaxone 1 g IV once and azithromycin 500 mg IV once.

plan: Admit to step-down for oxygen titration, goal SpO2 at least 92%
No further antibiotics beyond the ED doses
Prednisone 40 mg PO daily starting tomorrow morning (was 5 mg daily)
Stop MTX; rheumatology to decide on an alternative DMARD
Continue hydroxychloroquine 200 mg BID, omeprazole 20 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily
Start TMP-SMX DS 1 tab MWF for PJP prophylaxis while on prednisone 20 mg or more
TTE to evaluate RV function; BMP and CBC in the morning
Inpatient rheumatology consult; PFTs with DLCO once stable
Pillbox and phone alarms for medications around shift changes; pharmacy to give a written medication list
Flu and pneumococcal vaccines before discharge if not up to date

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. Tell me what is going on with the knee.
Patient: It's my right knee. It has been getting worse for about two years, and now it hurts every time I climb stairs or get up from a chair. In the morning it's stiff for maybe ten minutes.
Doctor: How bad is the pain on a scale of zero to ten?
Patient: About six on most days, and eight after a long walk.
Doctor: Any swelling, locking, or giving way?
Patient: Some swelling after I walk, but it doesn't lock and it doesn't give way. No fever, and no redness. Just an achy pain.
Doctor: Any injury to it?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: What have you been taking for it?
Patient: Naproxen 500 mg twice a day, and I get heartburn from it. I also take lisinopril 20 mg once a day for high blood pressure.
Doctor: Just to confirm, you are a 69-year-old male, correct, and no kidney problems?
Patient: Right, 69. My kidneys are fine as far as I know.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 146/88 with a heart rate of 74, and your weight is 212 pounds, which gives a BMI of 31. The standing X-rays you had last week show moderate narrowing of the inner joint space of the right knee with bone spurs, and no fracture. On exam there is a small effusion, tenderness along the medial joint line, and crepitus with motion. You can fully straighten it and bend it to 120 degrees. The knee is stable and not warm, and there is no calf tenderness.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is osteoarthritis of the right knee, what some people call wear and tear arthritis. Because of your blood pressure and the heartburn, I want you to stop the naproxen. Anti-inflammatory pills can raise blood pressure and irritate the stomach. Instead, use diclofenac 1% gel on the knee four times a day, and acetaminophen 650 mg three times a day as needed. Today I would also like to give a corticosteroid injection into the knee, triamcinolone 40 mg with lidocaine, for relief over the next few weeks.
Patient: Okay, let's do that.
Doctor: All done with the injection. Keep the spot clean and dry for a day. I will also refer you to physical therapy for strengthening, and losing even ten pounds will take pressure off the joint. Keep taking the lisinopril and check your blood pressure at home. Come back in 6 weeks, and if the knee is not better we will talk about other options.
Patient: Sounds good.
summary: A 69-year-old male has had two years of worsening right knee pain with brief morning stiffness and swelling after walking, without locking, giving way, fever or redness. He takes naproxen 500 mg twice a day, which causes heartburn, and lisinopril 20 mg once a day for high blood pressure, which measured 146/88 today. Standing X-rays show moderate medial joint-space narrowing with bone spurs and no fracture, and the exam shows a small effusion and medial joint line tenderness. The diagnosis is osteoarthritis of the right knee. Naproxen is stopped in favor of diclofenac 1% gel and acetaminophen, a triamcinolone injection was given today, and physical therapy and a 6-week follow-up are arranged.

soap.subjective: 69-year-old male with about two years of worsening right knee pain, worse with stairs and rising from a chair, 6 out of 10 most days and 8 after long walks, with morning stiffness of about ten minutes and some swelling after walking. No locking, giving way, fever, redness or injury. Taking naproxen 500 mg twice a day with heartburn, and lisinopril 20 mg once a day for high blood pressure. No known kidney problems.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 146/88, heart rate 74, weight 212 pounds, BMI 31. Standing X-rays: moderate narrowing of the medial joint space of the right knee with bone spurs, no fracture. Exam: small effusion, tenderness along the medial joint line, crepitus, full extension and flexion to 120 degrees, stable knee, not warm, no calf tenderness.
soap.assessment: Osteoarthritis of the right knee. High blood pressure. Heartburn on naproxen.
plan: Stop naproxen
Diclofenac 1% gel to the knee four times a day
Acetaminophen 650 mg three times a day as needed
Corticosteroid injection of the knee with triamcinolone 40 mg and lidocaine, done today
Refer to physical therapy for strengthening and counsel on weight loss
Continue lisinopril and check blood pressure at home
Follow up in 6 weeks

symptoms.text: tenderness along the medial joint line

note:
54-year-old female seen in ED, endocrine consulted, known postmenopausal osteoporosis, now s/p fall w/ wrist injury.
CC: L wrist pain and deformity after fall at home 4 h ago.
HPI: tripped on rug, FOOSH, fell from standing height. Denies head strike, LOC, neck pain, hip pain, back pain, numbness/tingling in the hand.
Dx'd w/ osteoporosis 1 y ago on DXA (spine T-score -2.8, L femoral neck -2.4), started on alendronate but unsure how she takes it.
Limited health literacy: relies on daughter to read labels, could not say which pill is "for the bones." Per pt takes alendronate "w/ breakfast and coffee" and lies back down after. Teach-back + picture cards used throughout visit.
PMH: postmenopausal since age 50, GERD, vit D deficiency.
Meds PTA (confirmed w/ pharmacy fill hx): alendronate 70 mg weekly, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
NKDA.
Vitals: BP 132/78, HR 88, RR 16, T 36.8 C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Exam: L wrist swollen w/ dorsal deformity, TTP distal radius, radial pulse intact, cap refill < 2 s, sensation intact.
No bony tenderness over spine, pelvis or hips.
Labs: Ca 9.2, Cr 0.8, eGFR 88, 25-OH vit D 14 ng/mL (low), PTH 62, TSH 1.8.
Imaging: wrist XR shows closed distal radius fx, dorsally displaced.
ED course: splint + sling placed, acetaminophen 650 mg PO x1 for pain w/ relief. Ortho consulted.
Imp:
- fragility fracture (distal radius) in setting of postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk
- vit D deficiency
- likely incorrect alendronate use r/t limited health literacy; GERD
Plan:
- STOP alendronate (taken incorrectly, GERD)
- plan zoledronic acid 5 mg IV once yearly as outpatient after vit D repleted + dental check
- start vit D3 2000 IU daily and calcium carbonate 600 mg BID w/ meals
- continue omeprazole 20 mg daily
- acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN pain
- ortho f/u in 1 wk for fracture mgmt
- endocrine clinic f/u in 4 wk w/ repeat 25-OH vit D
- fall prevention: remove loose rugs, home safety PT eval
- written pictogram med list + pillbox, daughter given copy; teach-back done
summary: A 54-year-old female with known postmenopausal osteoporosis and limited health literacy presented to the ED after a fall from standing height with a left wrist injury. She denies head strike, LOC, and neck, hip or back pain, and the wrist X-ray shows a closed, dorsally displaced distal radius fracture. 25-OH vit D is low at 14 ng/mL. The impression is a fragility fracture from postmenopausal osteoporosis with likely incorrect alendronate use and vit D deficiency. The wrist was splinted, alendronate is stopped, vit D3 and calcium carbonate are started, and zoledronic acid is planned after vit D is repleted, with ortho and endocrine follow-up.

soap.subjective: 54-year-old female with known postmenopausal osteoporosis, diagnosed 1 year ago on DXA, presenting with left wrist pain and deformity after tripping on a rug and falling from standing height 4 hours ago. History of GERD and vit D deficiency, postmenopausal since age 50. Takes alendronate 70 mg weekly and omeprazole 20 mg daily. No known drug allergies.

Left wrist swollen with dorsal deformity, tenderness over the distal radius, radial pulse intact, cap refill under 2 seconds, sensation intact; no bony tenderness over spine, pelvis or hips. Labs: Ca 9.2, Cr 0.8, eGFR 88, 25-OH vit D 14 ng/mL (low), PTH 62, TSH 1.8. DXA: spine T-score -2.8, left femoral neck -2.4. Wrist XR: closed distal radius fracture, dorsally displaced. Splint and sling placed and acetaminophen 650 mg given with relief.
soap.assessment: Fragility fracture of the distal radius in the setting of postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk. Vit D deficiency. Likely incorrect alendronate use related to limited health literacy; GERD.
plan: Stop alendronate
Plan zoledronic acid 5 mg IV once yearly as an outpatient after vit D is repleted and a dental check
Start vit D3 2000 IU daily and calcium carbonate 600 mg BID with meals
Continue omeprazole 20 mg daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN for pain
Ortho follow-up in 1 week for fracture management

Written pictogram medication list and pillbox, copy given to daughter, teach-back done

note:
Doctor: Hi, I understand you were told to come in because your left leg is still swollen?
Patient: Yes. I had a clot in my left leg six weeks ago, and I'm on the blood thinner. The calf is still swollen and sore, and it got worse over the last two days.
Doctor: And you are a 50-year-old male, right? Remind me what led to the clot.
Patient: Yes, 50. I broke my left ankle and was in a cast for five weeks, and then they found the clot.
Doctor: Which blood thinner do you take, and how do you take it?
Patient: Apixaban, 5 mg twice a day. They started me on a higher dose for the first week, then 5 mg.
Doctor: Have you missed any doses?
Patient: Maybe two in the last week. I forget the evening one sometimes.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath, and I haven't coughed up any blood.
Doctor: Any bleeding, like black stools, nosebleeds, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No, nothing like that. But I've been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the leg.
Doctor: Okay. Anything else you take?
Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg once a day for high blood pressure.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 134/82, heart rate 80, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.9. On exam the left calf is mildly swollen and tender, about 2 centimeters larger than the right, with no redness or warmth. The foot is warm with normal pulses, and your lungs are clear. We did a leg ultrasound with Doppler here. It shows the clot in the left popliteal vein is still there but smaller, with no new extension and no clot in the other veins.
Patient: So the blood thinner is not working?
Doctor: It is working. Some swelling and soreness is normal for weeks. This is a deep vein thrombosis that was provoked by the cast, and it is improving. The ibuprofen is the problem, because it raises your bleeding risk with apixaban, so please stop it. Take acetaminophen 500 mg, two tablets up to three times a day as needed, instead. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice a day and do not skip the evening dose, so set a phone alarm. Wear a knee-high compression stocking during the day. I will refer you to hematology to decide how long to continue treatment, probably three months in total since it was provoked. Go to the emergency room for chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, or black stools.
Patient: Okay, I will.
summary: A 50-year-old male on apixaban for a left leg deep vein thrombosis diagnosed 6 weeks ago after cast immobilization for an ankle fracture presents with calf swelling and soreness that worsened over two days. Doctor: Welcome back. I have the discharge summary from your hospital stay three weeks ago. Let me confirm, you are a 31-year-old male with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump, correct?
Patient: Yes. I was admitted for two nights after I passed out from a low. My roommate found me confused and gave me glucagon, and the ambulance took me in.
Doctor: How have things been since you got home?
Patient: I'm still having lows, mostly at night between two and four in the morning, and a few after I play basketball. Some nights I wake up sweaty and shaky.
Doctor: Any seizures or passing out since discharge?
Patient: No seizures and no passing out. No vomiting or belly pain either, and no extra thirst.
Doctor: Good. Any problems with the pump site, like redness or infection?
Patient: No, the sites are fine.
Doctor: What insulin is in the pump, and what are your settings?
Patient: Insulin lispro. My overnight basal is 0.9 units per hour, and my carb ratio is 1 to 10.
Doctor: And you also take something for your thyroid?
Patient: Levothyroxine 100 mcg every morning, for Hashimoto's.
Doctor: I reviewed your pump download and sensor data today. Your average sensor glucose is 128 and your A1c is 6.4%, but you spend 14% of the time below 70, and the lows cluster between 2 and 4 in the morning. Your blood pressure is 118/72 and your weight is 78 kilograms. Your pump sites look clean with no redness.
Patient: So my numbers are good?
Doctor: The average is excellent, but there are too many lows. This is type 1 diabetes with frequent hypoglycemia, most likely from an overnight basal rate that is too high plus exercise. I am lowering your overnight basal from 0.9 to 0.7 units per hour from midnight to 5 AM. For basketball, use a temporary basal reduction of 50 percent starting one hour before. I am also prescribing nasal glucagon 3 mg, one spray in one nostril for a severe low, and I want your roommate to learn how to give it. Please check your glucose before driving. We will review a new download in 4 weeks.
Patient: Okay, I will do that.

Telehealth video visit for aortic stenosis surveillance. The patient is a 78-year-old male connected from home with a stable video connection; identity and location were confirmed and he consented to the video visit.

Reason for visit: routine follow-up of aortic stenosis first found as a heart murmur. His last echocardiogram 6 months ago showed an aortic valve area of 1.3 cm2, a mean gradient of 28 mmHg and a normal ejection fraction.

Interval history: he reports no chest pain, no fainting or near-fainting, and no shortness of breath when walking up one flight of stairs. He also has no palpitations or leg swelling. He drinks about five beers a day, which he acknowledges is heavy alcohol use. He has hypertension treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily.

Home measurements: blood pressure 136/78 and heart rate 70 on his home cuff, and weight stable at 182 pounds.

Video exam: he appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences, with no cyanosis or visible distress and no visible leg swelling. Heart auscultation could not be performed by video.

Impression: aortic stenosis, asymptomatic and stable by history, with heavy alcohol use and hypertension.

Plan: repeat echocardiogram in 6 months. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. Start thiamine 100 mg daily. I counseled him to cut back on alcohol and referred him to alcohol counseling. He should call or go to the emergency department for chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath. Follow-up video visit after the echocardiogram.

Dermatology inpatient progress note, hospital day 2, for a 20-year-old female admitted with a severe flare of atopic dermatitis. She returned about 1 week ago from a 3-week trip abroad, and the flare worsened during the trip in hot, humid weather, with widespread itching, redness and loss of sleep. She has a history of mild asthma. She denies fever, denies pain or oozing from the lesions, and has used no new skin products other than a sunscreen she bought during the trip. She reports that the itching is better after the first night of wet wrap therapy.

On exam she is comfortable. Vitals: temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 112/68. Skin shows diffuse red scaly plaques with excoriations over the neck, antecubital and popliteal fossae, and trunk, covering about 35% of the body surface area. There is no honey-colored crusting, no pustules, and no punched-out erosions to suggest secondary infection.

Impression: severe flare of atopic dermatitis, improving on inpatient treatment, without signs of secondary infection. Her mild asthma is stable.

Plan: continue triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the body, avoiding the face, under wet wrap therapy. Continue cetirizine 10 mg at bedtime for itching. Use bland emollients liberally and stop the new sunscreen. Expect discharge tomorrow if the itching continues to improve, with dermatology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.

Hospital day 2 progress dictation on a 47-year-old male admitted with right lower extremity cellulitis. He also has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language and teach-back with him, and he needed pictures to understand his medication list. Overnight he had no fever. His pain is better. He denies chills, denies nausea or vomiting, and denies shortness of breath. He reports no chest pain. He has no known drug allergies.

Current medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain.

Vitals this morning temperature 37.2 Celsius, heart rate 82, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam the right lower leg has erythema and warmth over the shin and calf, with the erythema receding from the marked border by about 2 cm, correction, 3 cm. There is mild tender swelling but no fluctuance and no crepitus. There is no streaking up the thigh and pulses are intact.

Labs, white count 13.1 on admission and 9.4 today, creatinine 0.9, hemoglobin A1c 8.4%. Blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours. Venous duplex ultrasound of the right leg showed no deep vein thrombosis and no abscess.

Assessment is right lower extremity cellulitis, improving. Type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 8.4%, suboptimally controlled. Hypertension, stable.

Plan. Stop the IV cefazolin today and switch to cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily to finish a total of 7 days of antibiotics. Continue metformin and lisinopril. Acetaminophen as needed. Keep the leg elevated, and teach him to check his feet daily. Diabetes education using teach-back and simple picture handouts, and refer him to a diabetes educator. Primary care follow-up within 1 week. Discharge today if he tolerates the oral antibiotic.

He denies bleeding, denies pain, denies non-healing sores, and denies any lesion that has grown quickly. He gardens outdoors and has used sunscreen inconsistently. I counseled him that redness, crusting and irritation are expected during treatment and that this settles after he stops. In-person skin check in 6 weeks, with cryotherapy for any thick lesions. note:
Doctor: Good morning. What brings you in today?
Patient: I've had a stuffy nose and face pain for about twelve days. I thought it was a cold, and it got a little better around day five, and then it got worse again.
Doctor: Tell me more. Where is the pain?
Patient: Mostly over my cheeks and between my eyes, and it's worse when I bend forward. The mucus is thick and yellow-green, I have a bad taste in my mouth, and I have pressure in my upper teeth.
Doctor: Any fever?
Patient: I felt warm a few days ago, but I never took my temperature. No high fever, I think. No vision changes, no swelling around my eyes, and no stiff neck or bad headache.
Doctor: Good. I see in your chart that you're a 21-year-old male and you take a blood thinner. Which one is it?
Patient: Apixaban, 5 mg twice a day. I had a blood clot in my lung four months ago.
Doctor: Right, a pulmonary embolism. Any nosebleeds with this?
Patient: No nosebleeds.
Doctor: And what have you taken for the pain?
Patient: Ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a day.
Doctor: Do you have any allergies to medicines, especially antibiotics?
Patient: No, no allergies to any medicines.
Doctor: Your vitals today are temperature 37.9, blood pressure 124/76, heart rate 82, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. On exam you have tenderness over both maxillary sinuses, thick yellow-green drainage in the nose, and swollen nasal turbinates. Your throat is a little red without exudate, your ears look normal, your neck is supple, and your lungs are clear. The rapid COVID and flu test we did was negative.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is acute bacterial sinusitis, since you have had symptoms for more than ten days and then got worse. Because you are on apixaban, I need to be careful. Please stop the ibuprofen, since it raises bleeding risk with a blood thinner, and take acetaminophen 500 mg, two tablets every 6 hours as needed. I am starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice a day for 5 days. I am avoiding clarithromycin and fluconazole because they can raise apixaban levels. Also use saline rinses twice a day and fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, two sprays in each nostril once a day. Keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day. Call us if you get a high fever, vision changes, a severe headache, or a heavy nosebleed, and come back in a week if you are not better.
Patient: Okay, thank you.

He denies a high fever, vision changes, eye swelling, stiff neck, bad headache and nosebleeds, and he has been taking ibuprofen. Temperature is 37.9, with tenderness over both maxillary sinuses and thick yellow-green nasal drainage, and a rapid COVID and flu test was negative. The diagnosis is acute bacterial sinusitis. Ibuprofen is stopped in favor of acetaminophen, amoxicillin-clavulanate is started for 5 days, saline rinses and fluticasone are added, and apixaban continues.

plan: Stop ibuprofen because of bleeding risk with apixaban
Acetaminophen 500 mg, two tablets every 6 hours as needed
Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice a day for 5 days; avoid clarithromycin and fluconazole because they can raise apixaban levels
Saline rinses twice a day and fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, two sprays in each nostril once a day
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice a day
Call for high fever, vision changes, severe headache or heavy nosebleed; return in a week if not better
